patches.before:
Rscript test_orchestrator_workflow.R orchestrator_workflow.R

The tests check the shared demo schema, known QC values, metadata reordering, valid CPM, zero-library refusal, invalid counts and metadata, overwrite protection, and provenance output. Each output directory records a fixed local plan in plan.json, input and script content identifiers and R version in manifest.json, and status events in events.jsonl. A completed report ends at NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW. A hash identifies bytes; it does not establish source authenticity, dataset suitability, or scientific correctness.

Inspect files, units, sample identities, warnings, and study design before interpreting any real dataset. The workflow is not a security sandbox, a production pipeline, or an independent biological reviewer. Its calculations are descriptive, and software tests do not validate a research conclusion.

Optional Python implementation and provider exercise

The tested Python workflow and its tests remain available as an alternative for readers who prefer Python. The following original Python instructions are retained. They use Python-native tools and are not needed to run the R workflow above. The AI planner described there is optional and makes a real provider request only if you explicitly run that separate command; the R implementation makes no provider call.

1. Download and set up

Save both files into the same new folder. The workflow file is the full implementation, not a pseudocode fragment; the second file contains its automated tests.

patches.before:
1. Define the biological question. State whether the primary output is an assembly, structural-variant evidence, or transcript/isoform catalogue and quantification.
  2. Record the input contract. Note DNA or RNA, platform and read mode (for example HiFi, ONT cDNA, or direct RNA), basecaller where relevant, file type, and any preprocessing.
  3. Check reference compatibility. Record genome assembly accession/build and annotation release. Genome and annotation must describe the same coordinate system.
  4. Review QC and alignment. Save read-length/quality summaries, mapping summaries, and failed-read/filtering decisions. Report metrics rather than silently applying a universal threshold.
  5. Validate the interpretation. For assemblies, inspect contiguity and completeness indicators and unresolved regions. For variants or isoforms, inspect supporting reads and use orthogonal or independent evidence appropriate to the claim.

Exercise: choose and defend a route

Consider this hypothetical study: a laboratory has long-read RNA FASTQ files and wants to catalogue transcript structures. No organism, platform, basecaller, genome build, or annotation release is specified, so do not invent them. Draft a one-page plan with these fields: (1) questions to ask the data provider to identify molecule type and platform/read mode; (2) the exact genome build and annotation release you would require and how you would confirm their coordinate compatibility from provider metadata; (3) QC evidence to review; (4) a splice-aware alignment and isoform-analysis route, with read-type settings chosen only after the platform is confirmed; and (5) one independent validation source plus a limitation. Mark each unresolved item “pending” rather than selecting an arbitrary reference. A satisfactory plan names the missing evidence and explains why each decision depends on it; it does not claim a biological result. Stop before analysis if platform/read mode or genome/annotation compatibility cannot be established.

  • IsoQuant upstream documentation
  • PacBio HiFi sequencing overview
  • Oxford Nanopore documentation repository

Seurat's RPCA and CCA workflows find anchors between datasets rather than applying the same embedding-correction algorithm as Harmony. RPCA is described in Seurat's documentation as a more conservative alignment option; that general description does not predict which representation is appropriate for this dataset. Use the current integration vignette and RPCA guide for the API matching your object version.

To extend this experiment fairly, preserve the same selected cells, source labels and dimensions policy; record any method-specific preprocessing; align every branch by cell ID; rerun the same diagnostic calculations; and inspect original RNA markers and rare populations. Add RPCA/CCA rows only after those branches actually run. Different integration assays and corrected coordinates are not interchangeable with raw counts.

  • Seurat v5 integration overview; Single-cell best-practices integration chapter.
  • Upstream preparation: PBMC QC-to-clustering worked lab and QC decision guide. Annotation checks: the paired public annotation example.

patches.before:
Scope and tested boundary. This lesson evaluates supplied, precomputed cell embeddings. It does not load scGPT or Geneformer weights, run inference, generate embeddings, or infer regulatory networks. The included coordinates and labels are deliberately synthetic software-check data, not model outputs or biological evidence.

Use base R to validate embedding and metadata CSVs, align rows by cell ID, reject donor leakage, and evaluate donor-held-out cell-label transfer with squared-Euclidean k-nearest neighbors. The same question can be evaluated with the optional existing Python workflow. Model-specific embedding generation remains an upstream, separately documented step.

Format: Hands-on lab. R is the main route and uses only base R for local evaluation. R Markdown is an optional report wrapper. The only network operation in the companion files is the explicit protein-database retrieval lesson, not this evaluator.

On this page

  • Goal and assumptions
  • Upstream embedding handoff
  • Input contract
  • Run the R evaluator
  • Optional Python route
  • Interpret results and limitations
  • Model sources

Goal and assumptions

  • Check the exact CSV schema, unique cell identifiers, one-to-one identifier coverage, numeric finite coordinates, and metadata labels.
  • Keep all cells from each donor in one split and reject overlap between the reference and held-out test sets.
  • Run deterministic squared-Euclidean kNN; report accuracy, macro-F1, per-class F1, donor accuracy, neighbor IDs, distances, and top-vote fraction.
What you will produce. One predictions CSV and one metrics CSV. The top-vote fraction is neighbor agreement, not a calibrated probability. This is a small exact evaluator for teaching and modest tables, not a replacement for study-specific validation, Scanpy, scIB metrics, or biological review.

Upstream embedding handoff (not executed here)

Real model vectors must be generated separately with the exact official implementation, checkpoint, tokenizer/vocabulary, organism, preprocessing, embedding layer, and pooling documented for that model. Keep a record of those choices and the export provenance. Do not label toy vectors as scGPT or Geneformer output.

  • scGPT: use the official reference-mapping tutorial or integration tutorial. Check the chosen checkpoint and paired vocabulary and follow its actual preprocessing instructions; this lesson assumes no generic model API.
  • Geneformer: follow its official getting-started documentation and tokenization and embedding examples. Tokenization, gene identifiers, species, model version, and checkpoint differ from scGPT.

No pretrained output, model weights, inference code, GPU requirement, or heavyweight model installation is included or tested here. Donor holdout in this evaluator does not establish that a checkpoint never saw those donors or their study during pretraining.
